Section 14: Explaining the Characteristics of the Precepts; Section 15: Methods for Observing and Violating [the Precepts]; Section 16: The Dharma for Repenting the Six Classes of Offenses; Section 13: The Names and Rewards of the Categories of Offenses (Part 1 of 2). Regarding the "Names and Rewards of the Categories of Offenses," Section 13: The reason why the five groups who have left secular life serve as the excellent field of merit for the world is truly due to the essence of their precepts (*śīla*).
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Taking up and maintaining the prohibitive precepts constitutes its nature; shaving the hair and dyeing the robes constitute its marks.
Now, if one purifies the mind like ice and polishes virtue like jade, one can then produce the seeds of goodness and is designated as a "field of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Otherwise, if one stubbornly resists, one brings calamity upon oneself, incurs the guilt of the six categories of offenses, and is reborn in the prison of the twenty-eight hells.
Therefore, the five articles clarify transgressions, such that violating them constitutes a failure in observance;
the seven categories manifest observance, such that complying with them ensures that various transgressions are secretly eliminated.
Yet those among the newly initiated are for the most part dull-witted and ignorant;
not yet understanding the underlying principles, how could they discern the formal precepts?
They follow the prohibitions as blindly as one wandering through a mist, and their retribution for transgressions is like that of one gazing out at the ocean.
This causes one to drift along with the current, forgetting the way home in greed for a single drop of honey;
having committed grave karma, how could one transcend delusion to know how to turn back?
Thus, the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* says:
When monks and nuns violate the prohibitions yet receive offerings and sustenance, the reason they do not experience the retribution in the present life is that it is directed toward the hells!
Thus, karma is bound by the mind and retribution is formed by the mind;

one must first establish the principles of cause and effect and extensively clarify their characteristics and names, so that the sons of the Buddha who uphold the precepts may contemplate the fruit to understand the cause.
Among these, first the protection of the precepts is clarified as the primary cause of transgression;
subsequently, the characteristics of the retribution for the various categories of offenses are clarified.

Regarding the former: the reason why the karmic retribution for violating the precepts is so extremely grave is that the protection of the precepts is the most supreme among the cultivation of wholesome dharmas and establishes the strongest merit.
Therefore, to cause such violation and loss is to invite a heavy retribution.
The *Vidyāmātra-śāstra* (or *Prakaraṇābhidharma*) describes many types of guarding the precepts; I shall briefly cite them here.
That which resides in the mind is termed "guarding" (*ārakṣā*).
That which pertains to body and speech is called "precept" (*śīla*).
There may be protection without necessarily being a precept, but where there is a precept, it is necessarily protection, and so forth.
In the sūtras, the Buddha praises those who have attained both the precept and its protection; there are many passages on this subject, of which eight types are briefly described as follows:
First, it is like a king who has fathered a son who is revered by the people;
having obtained the precepts that protect one, one is born into the lineage of the noble ones and will certainly attain sainthood hereafter, just as the prince succeeds to the royal throne.
Second, just as the light of the moon gradually becomes full, so too is the protection of the precepts:
all virtues and such increase according to the occasion, until one attains the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Third, it is like a person who obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel: whatever they desire is fulfilled;
likewise, one who obtains the protection of the precepts will certainly be able to attain birth in the happy realms and even reach Bodhi, according to their aspirations.
Fourth, it is like a king’s only son, whom he cherishes for the sake of his succession to the throne;
so too, one who has obtained the precepts that protect a person must cherish them because those precepts lead inevitably to the attainment of sainthood, and they must not be violated or damaged.
Fifth, it is like a person who has but one eye and cherishes it most deeply;
this person is likewise, for by guarding the precepts, they shall escape birth and death and attain nirvana.
Sixth, just as a poor person in the world cherishes even a small amount of provisions, because of this love for the precepts, one obtains the life of wisdom.
Seventh, just as a king who possesses three things loves his kingdom: first, wealth; second, sensual objects; and third, the true Dharma.

The same applies to one who has attained the protection of the precepts: dwelling within the protection of the precepts, one possesses immeasurable merit, the mind is peaceful and free from remorse, and the True Dharma grows.
Eighth, it is like a sick person obtaining excellent medicine;
the protection of the precepts is likewise, and one should not abandon it, for by means of it, one is freed from all evil.
Such being the causes and conditions, the merit and the task are profound and grave;
one must not lightly transgress them, for to do so incurs great sin.
Second, the listing of names and the explanation of their positions.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the categories and clusters (*pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, etc.); second, the explanation of the karmic retributions.
Regarding the first part: the five categories (*pañca-varga*) and seven clusters (*sapta-nikāya*) are differentiated according to their respective meanings.
In establishing the formal categories of offenses, only six types of rules are set forth.
Now, following these six groups (*ṣaḍ-varga*), I shall briefly explain their names:
first, *pārājika*; second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, *sthūlātyaya* (or *sthūlātyaya*); fourth, *pāyattika* (or *pāyattika*); fifth, *pratideśanīya*; and sixth, *duṣkṛta*.
These six names above have no direct translations;
they are merely rendered according to their meaning so that one may gain a rough understanding of their general path.
First, regarding the term *pārājika*:
The meaning of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is that this constitutes an extreme evil.
It is explained through three points:
first, it is "retrogression and sinking," because by violating this precept, one has no share in the fruits of the Path.
Second, they no longer dwell together; it is not merely that they have lost the Way, but they further cease to be included within the two types of Saṃgha.
Third, they fall away; for after casting off this body, they will fall into the Avīci Hell.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Falling into an undesirable state.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* explains:
Because one fights against Māra, by violating this precept, one falls into defeat.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"A *pārājika* offense is like severing a person's head; they cannot rise again."
If one violates this rule, one no longer constitutes a bhikṣu;
therefore, this is named according to the practice performed rather than its formal designation.
Furthermore, it says:
"Pārājika" means "without remainder";
it is designated as such because one is severed from the communal Dharma;
thus the verse says:
"Those who commit evil deeds are like corpses, whom the community cannot tolerate; for this reason, one should uphold the precepts.

Furthermore, they are called "those who do not dwell together" because they are not permitted to dwell together with the two types of Saṃgha—namely, those who perform the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts) and the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts).
Question:
It was stated above that if one commits this offense, it is called "severing the head.
Judging by this, there can be no repeated commission of the offense, and thus the precept would not exist [as a continuing entity].
Answer:
Whether precepts exist or not is a matter that enters into contentious debate.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* explains it as follows:
There are precepts; they are not non-existent.
As for repeated offenses, the Vinaya provides its own clear adjudication:
according to the number of times one commits them, each constitutes a *pārājika*.

In this section, the first four precepts are distinct; depending on the gravity of the offense, one may commit sexual misconduct multiple times, and the same applies to repeated offenses of theft, killing, and lying.
This explains the Pratimokṣa precepts: because the objects and conditions differ, the attainment of the precepts varies accordingly.
Therefore, when a subsequent offense occurs, it follows the specific nature of that particular transgression.
As the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"It is better to receive all the precepts at once than to transgress all the precepts at once."

Furthermore, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct, twenty-one precepts are incurred in relation to a woman’s body, while fourteen precepts are incurred in relation to a man’s body; the same applies to men and women within the rest of the dharma-realm.
Now, if one has a greedy mind and violates the path of a single woman, it is merely called a defilement of the precept against sexual misconduct;

as for the bhikṣu’s other instances of sexual misconduct, the essence of his precepts remains radiant and pure, with no transgression of practice, and thus accords with the original essence received at ordination.
Just as when one repents for an offense of the first category, one regains purity;
it is not said that one must receive the precepts again, because the original precepts still exist.
Furthermore, as the Vinaya states:
If one slanders a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense (pārājika), one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
if the person slandered is not one who holds the precepts, it is merely a *duṣkṛta*.

Question: Should they be counted as fulfilling the quorum, or are they not considered "heads severed"?
Answer:

Since their fundamental transgressions have been purified through confession, they should logically fulfill the quorum, just as one who has attained [purification] may participate in the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* or the *Pravāraṇā*.
It is simply because their emotional afflictions are so deep and heavy that they are unfit for the service of the Sangha; thus it is said that "their coming does not accord with their wishes.
The admonition regarding "severing one's head" is spoken in the hope that they will not fail to attain the fruits of sainthood.
Question:
Although the precept against sexual misconduct may be defiled, it is still termed a "violation of the precepts. In what text does this appear? Answer: [The text follows].
This has already been clearly explained above;
its characteristics are further elaborated as described in the "Method of Repentance" (Chǎnfǎ) below:
the essence of the precepts is definitively established, eternally and constantly pure.

In this world, there are those who violate the precept against sexual misconduct; at first they are terrified, but later, reflecting upon it, they claim to have lost the precept and consequently follow suit in committing the transgression with others.
Is this not because, being ignorant of the net of the teachings, they have allowed themselves to sink into worldly custom?
How can one know that while committing only one instance of sexual misconduct, all other forms of lust are not being committed;
or that while engaging in killing and stealing as prescribed in the relevant chapters, one remains constantly pure and solemn;
or that the five groups of offenses below are governed by the same principles as the initial undertaking of the precepts?
Therefore, those of like dharma must clearly investigate this principle.
If one first purifies the consciousness and encounters the five sensory objects, desire and defilement will not arise, due to these preliminary expedients.
If one has not fundamentally restrained the mind, one cannot avoid transgressing when confronted with objects.
Once a transgression has occurred and karma is established, it must be unobscured; one must quickly eliminate even the slightest taint to restore original purity and re-enter the ranks of the Sangha.

If one is deluded regarding what has been established, harbors internal ailments within oneself, and does not participate in communal affairs, then both wealth and the Dharma will perish; if one then recklessly consumes these resources, bringing ruin to both self and others—is this not tragic!
Is this not a mistake?
Question:
If one has already been defiled by sexual misconduct yet all other precepts remain intact, why does one fail to attain the stage of a noble one (ārya)?
Answer:
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Vyākhyā*) explains:
"Regarding these four levels of precepts, if one violates even a single level, the remaining portions of the precepts will lack efficacy in their application."
Just as when a person dies, death occurs upon the impairment of any one of the four vital points;
so too, due to the weakness of the power of ethical discipline, meditative concentration and wisdom do not arise.
The *Daśacakra-sūtra* states:
"If one commits the four grave offenses, destroys the Dharma, or slanders the noble ones, upon death they will enter the Avīci hell;
such a person cannot exhaust their karmic fetters within a single lifetime and will inevitably fall into the evil realms."

If there are those who leave the household life within my Dharma, upholding the fundamental precepts and always exerting themselves with diligence and valor, they shall never receive any offerings in vain. Why is this?
Aiming for liberation, even at the cost of one's life, one shall never violate or destroy [the precepts].
Why is this? Because the four root [offenses] are that upon which the three vehicles rely and abide.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
nuns have eight *pārājika* offenses; the first four are identical to those of the bhikṣus, while the latter four are as explained in the "Separate" [section].
According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, repeated offenses are treated differently than in this Vinaya.
Regarding offenses of the same name, there is a possibility of repeated commission;
regarding offenses of the same kind, there is no such repetition.
This is stated according to the first section [of the Vinaya].

"If a śrāmaṇera who has committed an offense through training (*śaikṣa*) commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, he is made to undergo the *parivāsa* (concealment) procedure in sequence among the monks, followed by the six-night *mānāpya* (probation) for the removal of the offense.
Other details are as explained in other sections.
The *Viniścaya-śāstra* states:
"In the Vinaya, it is said that there are five categories of offenses.
The commentary explains:
This section serves as a chapter.
Now, following the original meaning, I establish the title of this division.
There are two meanings:
First, the meaning of the fundamental [offenses]; second, the meaning that accords with the fundamental [offenses].
Regarding the first, the *Pārājika* section, there are sixteen offenses.
The explanation states:
Each of these has four stages, constituting sixteen offenses.
First is the remote preliminary (*dūre-prayoga*): for example, when engaging in sexual misconduct, first giving rise to the intention without yet moving body or speech;
if one reproaches the mind, it is extinguished.
The second is the secondary preparatory act (*anuprayoga*), which refers to moving the body toward the object or speaking with the mouth of one's intention to act;
this is extinguished through confession before another person;
it is collectively termed a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
The third preparatory stage (*upakrama*) occurs when one approaches another person, perhaps wishing to touch them; before physical contact has occurred, this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one touches the person with the intent to engage in sexual intercourse, rather than for the sake of mere play or pleasure, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* and does not constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
this offense is to be confessed before another person.
The fourth, physical union, is the fundamental act.
The preceding three are preparatory stages; because they serve to bring about its accomplishment, they are called "sections" (kula).
If the fundamental act has not yet been accomplished, the preceding three may be confessed.
If [the offense] has already been accomplished, the first three types follow their respective roots and are entirely incapable of repentance;
this is the meaning of "conformity" (*anuvartana*).
The remaining three categories follow this same principle.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is simply stated that if [the act] is accomplished, it is a *pārājika*; if not accomplished, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one follows the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (*Daśabhāṇavāra*), however, the *sthūlātyaya* is divided into heavy and light degrees.
In the *Viniścaya-śāstra*, only one chapter is concluded.
However, as for the nature of *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta*, they apply to both [the *Vinaya-sūtra* and the *Viniścaya-śāstra*];
this should be understood through analogical interpretation, as further explained in the "Chapter on Repentance" (*Prāyaścitta*).
The second is the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* category.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"Saṃgha" means for the Saṃgha;...
The term *pā* refers to the beginning, meaning the *saṃgha-pūrva-āvaraṇa-karman* (the formal act of concealment) granted before the Saṃgha;
the term *śeṣa* means "remainder," referring to the final *āpatti-vyutthāna-karman* (the formal act of emerging from the offense).
If one commits this offense, it is named after its objective basis because it is removed through a formal act of the Saṃgha.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Saṃgha" means for the community; "pārājika" refers to those who have fallen away; "saṃghāvaśeṣa" means residual.
If one commits this offense, the defilement entangles the practitioner, and it is not a completely pure application.
This is because the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (requiring suspension) is eliminated through the Saṃgha.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the section precisely clarifying the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses constitutes the preceding explanation.
It is further said that "having a remainder" (sa-avaśeṣa) is a designation for the fact that the practice of the Dharma is not yet severed.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
"Saṃghāvaśeṣa means that it is like a person who has been cut by another; because a throat remains, it is called 'remainder' (śeṣa)."
It is necessary to provide rescue early.
Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"If one commits this offense, one should be compelled to undergo *parivāsa* and other penances, because it is a grave offense."
If categorized by their types, there are thirteen for monks, as explained in the "Following Characteristics" [chapter];
for nuns, there are seventeen, with six differences and seven similarities, as detailed in the "Specific Explanations."
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains:
The second section, the Saṃghāvaśeṣa, consists of fifty-two offenses.
Various schools offer differing explanations regarding these offenses.
This refers to the Saṃmitīya school, whose name has three meanings;
the Sarvāstivāda school calls it *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, which has one meaning identical to that of the Saṃmitīya school.
The commentary explains:
The meaning of *saṃgha* (the community) arises from the harmonious union of precepts (*śīla*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the assembly of persons.

Because these two [sets of precepts] differ, and because they do not arise from concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), but rather from the precepts established by the Buddha, it is said that their precepts are identical.
Because they share the same right view, it is said that their views are identical.
*Pārājika* (Sanskrit; Pācittiya/Pārivāsika in this context) means "residual" (*śeṣa*).

If one commits this offense, one must undergo disciplinary confinement within the Sangha; dwelling among the senior, middle, and junior monks, one remains at the very outer edge, and is therefore called "residual."
*Mānatva* is translated as "pleasing the minds of the assembly";
by complying with the instructions of the Saṃgha, all harbor joy.
*Ābhāṣaṇa* is translated as "calling one to enter the assembly."
Regarding the three meanings of *pāṭidesanīya* according to the Saṃmitīya school, the first is as explained previously.
The second is the meaning of "rescue," which means that by being saved by the Saṃgha, one is able to escape this offense.
Third is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*): when one is on the verge of committing an offense, one becomes an inferior person;
through the deliverance provided by the Saṃgha, one regains purity and attains excellence from that inferior state.
Third is the *sthūlātyaya* category.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"Sthūla" means great; "atyaya" means obstructing the path to wholesome states."
Later, one falls into the evil realms, where the body is base and defiled;
as for establishing a name based on this unwholesome nature, it is because one is capable of committing the offenses of the first two categories.
Furthermore, it is translated as "grave offense" (*tài-zuì*), and is also called "coarse and evil."
The *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* states:
"The correct pronunciation is called *satthula*.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains:
*Thūlaccaya* (sthūlātyaya) refers to the coarse; *pārājika* (pācittiya) refers to the transgression.
There are two kinds of coarseness:
first, the preliminary stage (*prayoga*) of a grave offense; second, that which is capable of severing the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
What is called a transgression refers to failing to act in accordance with the precepts established by the Buddha; thus it is called a transgression.
It is like an ox breaking through a fence or enclosure; one has thereby strayed outside the domain of the renunciant.
However, the designation "transgression" (āpatti) applies universally.
This offense is termed a transgression at its initial commission; subsequent instances receive their name from that first occurrence.
It is like a later cow following the lead of the first: it too is considered to have crossed the boundary.
However, the category of sthūlātyaya (grave offense) spans both primary and derivative offenses, its nature encompassing both light and heavy degrees;
since the Vinaya lists seven categories and six categories,
both of which include sthūlātyaya— whether positioned at the beginning or the end— it is for this reason that such is the case.

In the Vinaya, those offenses that follow after the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṅghādisesa) are so categorized because they are subsumed under the category of "offenses" (*śīla-skandha*) and their criminal gravity is heavy;

these include, for example, the preparatory stages (*prayoga*)—both distant and proximate—and the principal offenses (*maula-āpatti*) of the first two categories, such as causing schism in the Saṃgha, theft, and the four [grave offenses].
Alternatively, if it occurs under the *tissaṇī* (pāyantika) offenses, it is subsumed under matters of decorum (*airyāpathika*), and the offense is minor;

this refers, for example, to the remote preliminary stages (*dūre-prayoga*) of the second category of offenses, as well as minor independent offenses (*mukhya-apatti*), such as the cases of using one's hair while naked, and so forth.
However, regarding precepts (*śīla*) and dignified demeanor (*airyāpatha*), they may be cited either collectively or individually.
Taken collectively, "precepts" refers to the precepts themselves; even when they are not manifest as dignified demeanor, any violation is termed a breach of the precepts.

If discussed according to their individual distinctions, the first three categories (*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and *sthūlātyaya*) involve transgressions that are coarse and prominent; thus, that which can govern them is called "precept."
The latter four offenses are minor; the conduct capable of remedying them is termed "dignified deportment" (īryāpatha).
If categorized according to their uniformity or mixture: the former four are uniform, as they are exclusively non-virtuous results;
the latter three are mixed, encompassing both minor offenses and their causes.
However, the *sthūlātyaya* is the most serious among the miscellaneous offenses; therefore, it is placed fifth.
The fourth category consists of the *pāyattika* (Pāli) or *pāyittiya* (Sanskrit), which is translated as "falling" (*patati*).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Because they fall into the hell of burning, boiling, and obscuration.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:

There are one hundred and twenty types of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; thirty of these are categorized as arising from matters of property, where greed and arrogance are strong, and thus they must be relinquished to the Saṃgha—hence they are called *niḥsargika*.
The remaining ninety are to be confessed individually to another person;
however, according to the nature of the offense itself, they constitute a single category of confession.
The two hundred and eight precepts for bhikṣuṇīs are entered into the third section;
the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses and the remainder are entered into the separate confessions (*pratyekadeśanā*).
The similarities and differences in their categories and characteristics are as revealed in the [Prātimokṣa] Sūtra on Separate Confessions.
The *Vinayamukha-vinaya* states:
"Nissaggiya" was formerly translated as "shedi-duo" (捨墮).
The *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* states:
*Ni* is translated as "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*);
*sargi* means "to abandon" (*pratyādeśa*);
and *pāyattika*—its original name being *pāyatti*, pronounced with the *yi* and *ge* reversed—is "to bring about" (*nī*).
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* explains:
In the Sarvāstivāda school, there are three hundred and sixty offenses (*pārājika*).
In the Saṃmitīya school, it is translated as "that which should be applied" (*saṃprayukta*), which is interpreted through three meanings:
First, there are many minor and subtle offenses that are difficult to recognize and easy to disparage.
Second, there are natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*).
Third, regarding those who are prone to violating precepts, one should apply effort as an antidote so that such transgressions do not proliferate.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* states:
*Pārajika-vaicittika* is translated as "requiring immediate counteraction";
one must constantly reflect so that, should a transgression occur, it is immediately recognized.
The Theravādins say:
*pācittiya* is translated as "that which can burn and heat";
this offense results in rebirth in the Mahāraurava Hell.
At the time of the cause, it can scorch and heat the mind; at the time of the fruit, it can burn sentient beings.
There are three categories and two methods.
Thirty and ninety thus make one hundred and twenty.
There is no *sthūlātyaya*; there are two *duṣkṛta*s.
There is the group of five *prādeśanīya* offenses.
The meaning is translated as "confessing toward another"; the name is established based on the object of the remedial action (*pratipakṣa*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"This offense should be confessed.
This refers to the words for repentance clearly set forth in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* of this Vinaya.
There are four types of *bhikṣus*, as detailed below;
there are eight types of *bhikṣuṇīs*, which differ entirely from those of the *bhikṣus*.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Vyākhyā*) explains:
The fourth section, the *pāṭidesanīya*, consists of twelve offenses;
these are to be confessed individually by speaking to another person regarding the action committed.
The six groups of *dukkaṭa* (offenses of wrong-doing).
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Dukka" means evil;
"ṭa" means [the act of] doing. Thus, it refers to an evil deed.
*Gila* means "to do.
According to the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra*, its correct pronunciation is *tudu-muò-xī-jí-lì-duō*.
In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is called *śikṣākaraṇī*.
The meaning is translated as "that which should be studied";
the Hu monks say it means "guarding the precepts.
This offense is subtle and extremely difficult to maintain; therefore, it is named according to the practice of studying and guarding it at every step.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"With the divine eye, one sees offending bhikṣus as thickly as falling rain.
Is this not to say that when one focuses exclusively on the practice within the mind, it is called 'guarding the precepts'?
In this Vinaya, there are one hundred rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*); for the nuns, these rules are indicated as being the same as those for the great monks (*bhikṣu*).
Among the seven groups of offenses (*āpatti-skandha*), this one category is divided into two groups:

If there are those who, for their own sake, desire to seek the Buddha-way, they should revere the True Dharma; this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
Therefore, the compilation of the Tripiṭaka was the very first of these teachings.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"The Vinaya-piṭaka is the life-span of the Buddha-dharma; as long as the Vinaya-piṭaka endures, the Buddha-dharma will endure. Therefore, it was codified first."
The reason for this is that other sutras merely provide a general clarification of the traces of transformation and universally manifest cause and effect; therein,
phenomena follow from the principle, and the words have no fixed point of reference.
The meaning is indeed profound and far-reaching, yet my deluded mind has not yet attained it;
though I wish to advance in practice, I rarely grasp its essentials,
for I am often stalled by the traces of words due to my confusion regarding the intent of the teachings.
Now, the great treasury of the precepts and discipline is maintained through strenuous effort;
yet all that is currently being constructed or produced is coarse and superficial.
This is because, in terms of persons, their physical forms and attire differ from those of other ages, while in terms of the Dharma, its regulations and applications possess specific formalities.
Since their dwelling is already different from that of the laity, their various practices are distinctly separate.
Because the world exists through following signs and phenomena are established by pursuing signs,
they are thus able to provide a guiding framework so that the teaching does not fall to the ground.
Furthermore, the Dharma can support people and personally bring about the accomplishment of all practices, enabling people to propagate the Dharma;
thus, the Vinaya states:
"Because the community is in harmony, the Buddha-Dharma is able to endure for a long time."
Third, a brief explanation of the names and meanings.
According to the Sanskrit original, three names are established:
the first is *vinaya*, also called *vinaya* or *vinaya*, which is translated as "Vinaya" (Discipline).
Thus, within the eighteen dharmas of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the two terms "vinaya" and "lǜ" (律) do not function interchangeably;
furthermore, the *Ekottarika-āgama* speaks of seven kinds of vinaya, namely the seven vinayas.
Alternatively, some use "nirodha" (cessation) as a translation; however, naming it after its functional capacity is ultimately not a correct translation.
Therefore, translating it as "vinaya" (discipline) accords with the true meaning.
As for the term *śīla*, this is translated as "precept" (*jie*); that this refers to what is taught in the context of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) can be known from reliable evidence.
The third is called *prātimokṣa*, which here is translated as "liberation in each instance.
This reveals the sequence of the three [stages], which constitutes the beginning and end of a single transformation.
The Vinaya relies upon the teaching; since the teaching does not arise in isolation, it must explain the characteristics of practice, and the precepts (*śīla*) are established based upon this.
Precepts are not empty causes; they must inevitably yield their fruits. Therefore, liberation that severs all bonds stands foremost at the conclusion.
Next, its meaning shall be clarified.
First, it is said that "vinaya" means "dharma."
This refers to the dharmas of transgression and non-transgression, as well as their gravity and lightness;
these are all elucidated by the Vinaya, which constitutes the scriptural exposition.
Question:
The other two Piṭakas also clarify the practice of the Dharma; why then are they not specifically designated by name?
Answer:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The teachings expounded in the other Piṭakas primarily focus on meditative concentration and wisdom;
herein, however, it is proclaimed that the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*) serves as the foundational basis for all wholesome qualities.
Therefore, the name of the Dharma is first taken to induce and give rise to the latter two [perfections].
The reason for designating "Vinaya" first is that the five groups of renunciants differ from the world in their appearance and dress, thereby manifesting that their internal Dharma is also distinct.

However, because non-Buddhists and worldly laypeople indiscriminately conflate themselves with these holy traces, there is no way to distinguish them except through the subtle application of the Dharma;
therefore, the name "Vinaya" was first propagated to demonstrate the knowledge of the Dharma.
The rest is as explained in the usual commentaries.
Second is the meaning of *śīla* (precepts): as stated in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, it refers to the category that pervades the *dharmadhātu*.
This will be explained in detail later.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Precepts (*śīla*) are, in the language of Qin, 'inherent goodness' (*xing shan*).
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on Good Birth* (*Śāṅsheng jīng*) states:
"Precept" (śīla) means restraint; it restrains unwholesome dharmas.
Alternatively, it is said to mean "constriction," for its nature does not admit evil;
or it is said to mean "cooling," as its traces alleviate the heat of afflictions.
It may be called "superior" (śikṣā), for it enables one to ascend to the heavenly realms and reach the Unsurpassed Way;
this name is designated according to its functional efficacy.
Alternatively, it is distinguished from the perspective of the mind, as the Sūtra says: "It is training (śikṣā); it is training in the subduing of the mind," and so forth.
Alternatively, it may be understood according to its essential nature as being both manifest and unmanifest precepts; as the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"The discipline of individual liberation is virtuous by nature, not evil or indeterminate."
Regarding the correct principle of Hetuvidyā (Logic): "Precept" (*śīla*) refers to one's nature (*prakṛti*).
Since this nature permeates both good and evil, the non-restraint of evil (*akuśala-saṃvara*) likewise extends throughout all categories; therefore, it is called "non-discipline" (*asaṃvara*).
If these names are established in this way, "precept" (*śīla*) should mean that which restrains.
To restrain unwholesome dharmas for the sake of the wholesome is called "discipline" (*vinaya*);
to delight in killing from previous lives and act in accordance with such a dharma is called "ritual" (*vidhi*).
If one approaches it from the perspective of the wholesome restraint (*kuśala-saṃvara*), the reverse interpretation is precisely correct;
this thus establishes the name by deriving "discipline" (*vinaya*) from the teaching.
Furthermore, the Vinaya states:
*Vimokṣa* means precepts; this is a designation derived from the cause by way of the fruit.
As for the meaning of the three liberations (*vimokṣa*), they are proximate and manifest names, corresponding to the fruits according to their respective degrees.
That is to say, regarding the seven transgressions of body and speech, the conditions for their commission are not uniform;
by guarding against each one individually, one attains liberation according to their specific characteristics.
One draws near to the virtue of the precepts, and through the precepts, one achieves sainthood.
One aspires to sever all entanglements by adhering to the fundamental precepts.
Thus, the Vinaya states:
"By eliminating fetters, one becomes free from obstruction; through this, all bonds and attachments are liberated."
The rest is as explained below.
Regarding the four types of requisites, they differ;
however, if we speak of the final age, we discuss only the single reception through the *karmavācanā* ritual.
It must rely upon causes and depend upon conditions to be able to endure and flourish.
As for the characteristics of these conditions for receiving [the precepts], they are as explained in the first chapter of the preceding volume;
however, since this reception of the precepts is the great framework for a bhikṣu and the very foundation of the Buddha-dharma, I shall provide a further brief summary.
According to the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, five conditions must be fulfilled:
first, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) must be in accordance with the Dharma;
second, the two instructors (*ācārya*) must be in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, it is said that if one’s disciples have neither seen nor heard of any instance of breaking the precepts, they are fit to serve as teachers; this constitutes the limit for obtaining the precepts.
Regarding the purity of the *saṃgha* for three weeks:

this means that the three faculties (*indriya*) of the recipient are untainted, and with respect to all ten teachers, there is no one among them who has committed an illegal act—whether through seeing, hearing, or suspicion—only then can the reception of the precepts be successfully accomplished.

In the case of a *khaṇḍa* (partial) [ordination], there are three factors present, but the object does not constitute a full number, and the mind does not possess the requisite qualities; since one clearly knows it is not [valid], the *prātimokṣa* vow is not established.
Regarding the fourth, the accomplishment through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).
The treatise states:
"If the speech is incomplete, if the sequence of before and after is disordered, or if the explanation is not clear, it does not constitute a valid acceptance (*samanvāhāra*).
When the fivefold assembly of monks is in harmony, they grant their consent (*chanda*)."
If there are signs of a separate assembly as clarified in the *Pārivāsika-dharma*, the precepts cannot be received either.
Furthermore, it says:
if one who is a layperson receives the five precepts, the eight precepts, or even the ten precepts, and violates any one of the grave offenses;

Such a person, if they later leave the household life, will not obtain the precepts and may not serve as an upādhyāya; this is subsumed under the first of the thirteen obstacles (trayodaśa-antarāyika-dharma).
The remaining twelve obstacles are the same.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* states:

"If one has received the five precepts and violates one of the heavy [offenses], and subsequently renounces the five precepts to receive the five, eight, ten, or full (bhikṣu) precepts, as well as the dhyāna-precepts or the outflow-free (anāsrava) precepts, none of these will be obtained.
This applies even to the violation of a heavy offense among the eight precepts; one will not obtain them as before."
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:

"If one does not establish a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) outside the ordination platform (*sīmaṇḍala*), but instead establishes only a small boundary (*khuḍḍaka-sīmā*) directly, one may not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Even if there are currently circumstances of no obstacles, to receive ordination by establishing only a small boundary is likewise contrary to the Dharma."
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* further states:
"If one acts with a sincere and earnest mind, there is both the manifest action (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest action (*avijñapti*);
for one whose mind is frivolous and superficial, the unmanifest action is not produced."

Furthermore, if one receives [the precepts] and subsequently maintains them, this constitutes the correspondence between aspiration and practice; by relying on the treatises, one obtains the precepts.
If one receives [the precepts] but does not maintain them, there is merely an empty aspiration with no practice to correspond to it, and thus one does not obtain the precepts.
Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"One shares the same precepts as the bhikṣus.
Because one has received and maintains them in common with them, there can be persons who attain the precepts or who violate them.
Conversely, if one lacks the precepts, there is likewise no transgression.
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:
"When the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is concluded, does one obtain a wholesome mind?"
Question: Is it possible to obtain [the precepts] through an unwholesome mind, or even through a state of no-mind?
Answer: In all cases, this constitutes the attainment of the precepts.
If that is so, why does the Vinaya state:
"Those who are angry, drowsy, or insane—such persons as these are not said to have received full ordination"?
The answer is:
At the time of making the formal announcement (*jñapti*), although one possesses the aforementioned four mental states, it is not called "attaining the precepts";
only after the *karmavācanā* has been completed do the four mental states truly constitute the limit of attainment.

Regarding "the preceding wholesome mind not being obtained," this means that it generally takes other wholesome states as its object, but does not take the precepts as its object, nor is it analogous to other types of mindless states.
As for the five points of superiority and inferiority:

By establishing this gateway, one knows that the precepts are the supreme condition and the essential means for entering the Path; thus, one is able to maintain them without failing in their characteristics.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The *vimukti*-precepts exist while the Buddha is in the world, and because they appear rarely, they are superior."
The dhyāna-precepts and the outflow-free (anāsrava) precepts exist at all times.
The two types of outflowing (sāsrava) wooden-stick precepts apply to both sentient and non-sentient beings; because they are broad, they are said to be superior.
The other two [types] are restricted to sentient beings alone; because they are narrow, they are not as excellent.
The third, the prātimokṣa of the three outflows, is superior because it arises from a mind of loving-kindness and can serve as the cause for the Buddha-way.

As for the fourth, the prātimokṣa precepts, they extend to the seven assemblies and continue the Three Vehicles, the Three Jewels, and the Three Paths; their power to sustain and uphold [the Dharma] is formidable.
The other two are incapable of this and are therefore inferior.
The five *śīla* of the *prātimokṣa* exist only among the disciples of the Buddha;
as for other meditative precepts (*dhyāna-śīla*), even non-Buddhists possess them.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:

Regarding the one who is fully endowed with the *vinaya* (liberation): among all lights, all mountains, and all trainings, the light of the sun, Mount Sumeru, and the *vinaya* among trainings are considered the most supreme.
Were it not for the appearance of a Buddha, there would be no one to establish this Dharma.
Regarding the sixfold gravity of offenses:
according to the Sarvāstivāda school, precepts are not re-issued nor re-received, and offenses are not repeatedly committed; they remain fixed according to their original nature.
Therefore, the mind of an Arhat possesses middle and lower grades of precepts.
If this is so, why is it that some precepts are weak while others are not?
Answer:
Regarding these concurrent [factors], the substance of feeling is not considered.
Furthermore, it may be that the precept exists in a single moment, following a single grade of concentration;
whereas non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) is not of the mind, because it lasts for as long as one lives, its concurrent factors may increase or diminish.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
Someone asks, "Is there a re-issuance of the *prātimokṣa*?
The answer is: [Yes].
Within a single day, one may receive seven virtuous restraints (*śīla-saṃvara*);
wherever one attains the Path, one further acquires restraint;
yet that which was originally obtained is not lost, for the superior [restraint] receives the name.

The seven types of wholesome precepts refer to the five precepts, the eight precepts, the ten precepts, the full precepts, the dhyāna-precepts, the concentration-precepts, and the precepts concomitant with the Path.
As stated in the *Sarvāstivāda-śāstra-śiṣya-paramparā*:
"If one receives them again, they increase to become superior grades, yet the original summer retreat is not lost."
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* states:
In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, Huizhao and others of Qihuan Temple received the full precepts once again from the Indian monk Saṃghavarman.
Someone asked for the reason, and he replied:
"If one receives [the precepts] with doubt— whether as a person of middling or inferior capacity—
and subsequently seeks to attain further excellence, it is therefore necessary to receive them again."
According to the sequence of seniority based on one's original ordination age,
there were seven instances of receiving the precepts on Mount Zhenling.
I have heard some say that in this land, when receiving the precepts, there was originally no precedent to follow.
Even if those receiving [the precepts] today happen to lack a few auxiliary conditions, there is no reason to doubt that they have attained them in principle;
provided one maintains a mind of reverent adherence to the precepts, there is nothing that does not fall within the scope of attaining the precepts.
Upon suddenly hearing these words, I could not help but sigh deeply.
How could it be that because thunder shakes the earth, the deaf do not hear it;
or because the seven luminaries grace the heavens, the blind do not see them?
Since my understanding is limited like that of a small pipe, how could I dare to speak recklessly?
Therefore, the sacred teachings are cited to clarify this matter beyond doubt:
full ordination is accomplished when the requisite conditions are met, and cannot be obtained if they are lacking.
Regarding the full ordination in this land, it is clearly and extensively documented in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.

Even though there may be confusion regarding the objects of perception, there are clear instructions concerning the Dharma, as found previously in the section on "Receiving Precepts" in the preceding fascicle.

Regarding what is called "receiving the conditions for precepts within the Han realm": from the beginning of Emperor Ming’s dream at night until the arrival of Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna to transmit the Dharma, up until the early years of the Cao Wei dynasty, the monastic community was extremely flourishing, yet they had not yet received the full precepts of refuge.

They merely shaved their heads to distinguish themselves from the common people; even when they performed rites of fasting and repentance, these matters were identical to those of ancestral sacrifices.

Later, there was a monk from Central India named Dharmakāla (translated into Chinese as Fashí), who had recited the Vinayas of various schools. He arrived in Luoyang during the Jiaping era of the Wei dynasty;
he established the ritual of *karmavācanā* for ordination, marking the beginning of the Vinaya tradition in China.
Relying on a quorum of ten monks, he widely propagated the Buddha-dharma, rectified previous erroneous practices, and produced the *Sengqi jixin* (The Essential Precepts of the Mahāsāṃghika).
Furthermore, there was the śramaṇa Tandi from the country of Anxi, who was also well-versed in the study of the Vinaya;
he produced the *Dharmaguptaka Karmavācanā*, which marks the beginning of the formal procedures for receiving full ordination according to the Mahāsāṃghika school.

Regarding the initial circumstances for the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of bhikṣuṇīs: in the seventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, the Kasmirian śramaṇa Guṇavarman arrived in Yangzhou and translated the *Śīla-sūtra* and other scriptures.
Subsequently, eight nuns from Siṃhala arrived and said:
"In the land of Song, there have never before been bhikṣuṇīs; how can one receive the precepts through only two assemblies?"
Mopa said:
"If a nun does not perform the formal procedure according to the original method, she obtains the precepts but incurs an offense.

Following the intent of the Buddha's regulations, the dharma originates from the great assembly of monks; provided that the monastic procedure is successfully accomplished, one naturally obtains the precepts."
The reason for first having one perform the fundamental rite (*mūla-dharma*) is precisely to give rise to faith, serving as a preparatory means for receiving the precepts;
as for the actual attainment of the precepts, it occurs at the time of the formal *karmavācanā* ceremony conducted by the Great Sangha.
The bhikṣuṇīs earnestly requested that he receive [the precepts] again, to which he replied:
"Excellent!
As for the categories of morality, concentration, and wisdom, they progress from the subtle to the manifest; if you wish to increase their clarity, I am most pleased to comply."
Furthermore, he had the Western nuns learn the Chinese language and sent further invitations to nuns from China so that their number would reach ten.

In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era, there was one named Saṃghavarman (translated as "Multitude Armor"), who was proficient in the Vinaya and the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*; he traveled across the shifting sands and arrived in Yangzhou.
Initially, Gunavarman had consented to the re-ordination of nuns, but he passed away before the preparations were complete.

Shortly thereafter, three nuns from the Kingdom of Siṃhala, including Tiexuoluo (Lokeśvara), arrived at the capital; having determined that there were fewer than ten [monks] present, they requested the assembly headed by Tiexuoluo to serve as preceptors and performed the re-ordination for the nuns upon the altar.

I have extracted from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, the *Biographies of Famous Monks*, the *History of the Sangha*, the *Records of the Sangha*, as well as miscellaneous records of the Jin and Song dynasties.
Therefore, I have briefly set forth this account of its origins, to serve forever as a mirror for guidance.
Second is the essence of the precepts, which is divided into four sections: first, the characteristics of the essence of the precepts;

second, the similarities and differences between receiving and following them; third, the breadth and narrowness of the objects they encompass; and fourth, the number and quantity of the precepts generated.
The first five sections are as follows: first, distinguishing the number of essential natures;

second, establishing the two reasons for which [the name is given], thereby explaining its meaning; third, delineating the characteristics of the essential nature; fourth, the sequential arising of one from another; and fifth, the number of unmanifested [karmas].
At the beginning and middle [of my life], when it came to the Prātimokṣa precepts, everyone received them;
yet when it came to discussing clear understanding, there were only three or five.
This was entirely because I lacked innate intelligence and did not consult extensively.
This has caused the essence and characteristics of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) to become largely obscured;
they are merely objects formed within a blind dream-like mind, and when it comes to discussing their attainment, they remain as distant and vast as the Milky Way.
Therefore, at the beginning of the section on "Following Characteristics" (*anulakṣaṇa*), various gates are presented for demonstration.
One should first ascertain whether one has successfully attained the precepts within oneself; only then, regarding their observance or violation, may one cultivate detachment.
Question:
How many types of *pratimokṣa* (individual liberation) precepts are there?
Answer:
Regarding the substance of the treatise, it is immeasurable when considered in terms of its objects.
Since the root precepts prevent evil and the conditions for evil are numerous, the arising of these precepts is likewise numerous.
Therefore, the *Śāṅkhasmṛti* says:
"Sentient beings are immeasurable, and their precepts are likewise immeasurable," and so forth.
Now, by inferring through the meaning, they are essentially of only two kinds: manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*).
The two precepts encompass all [objects] such that none remain unexhausted.
Second, the establishment of two reasons, along with the explanation of the names and meanings.
Regarding the first: a question is asked:
"Why not establish only one, or perhaps three?
Answer:
If only "action" (kṛti) were established alone, once the substance of the action has passed away, it could not prevent wrongdoing, nor could it be maintained constantly.
Therefore, one must rely on non-informative action (*avijñapti*) to prevent wrongdoing over a long period.
If non-informative action were established in isolation, it would have no source from which it could arise;
it cannot manifest independently, but must depend upon informative action (*vijñapti*) for its production.
These two dharmas depend upon one another and cannot be established as two.
Why are they not three?
It is simply because their essential natures and characteristics are logically contradictory.
First, there is the distinction between the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and the conditioned; second, there is the distinction between the mind and what is not the mind.
Since their natures cannot be combined, only two [categories] can be established.
If one considers that which is to be prevented, they are infinite according to the objects [of restraint].
Second, regarding the citation of scriptural evidence: as the *Sarvāstivāda* [Abhidharma] states:
"If one acts with a sincere and earnest mind, there is no manifest instruction (*vijñapti*) of body or speech.
At the very first moment, there is the matter of bodily and vocal instruction, as well as non-instruction (*avijñapti*)."

In the second moment of thought, there is only the non-informative (avijñapti), and not the informative (vijñapti). "Informative" refers to action; it cannot be taught to others as something to be performed.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"There are two kinds of precepts:"
The first is the precept of action (*karmavirati*), and the second is the precept of non-action (*avijñapti*).
This person possesses only the precept of action and does not possess the precept of non-action; therefore, it is said that their precepts are incomplete.
As discussed above, because there is no sincere and earnest mind and no intention to practice accordingly, one does not give rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
Furthermore, the *Śāṅghabhadra-śāstra* states:
"Regarding these ten unwholesome paths of action, some consist only of informative action (*vijñapti*) and lack non-informative action."
There are instances of both manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) and non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
This is like the analogy of a person holding in their hand an object that is either extremely fragrant or foul-smelling, such as a tile or a piece of wood.
Among the various passages cited above, two points are not false.
Next, the meaning of the names is explained. Question:
Since the two types of precepts are already known, I request an explanation of their names.
The answer says:
That which is called "the agent" (kāraka) is like a potter’s wheel; when it moves and turns, it is designated as "acting.
Thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:
The "agent" refers to the body and the means of bodily movement.

To say there is no agent means that [the action] manifests continuously upon a single impulse, being present from beginning to end; the four types of mind and three natures do not depend on conditions for their discernment.
Thus, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* says:
Once bodily movement has ceased, this dharma continues to arise in conjunction with other consciousnesses; therefore, it is called "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, in the chapter on the "Unmanifest," states:
"Because sin and merit arise from the mind, they continue to arise constantly even during times such as sleep or fainting; therefore, they are called 'unmanifest'."
What is called "precept" (*śīla*)?
It is the restraint of unwholesome dharmas.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Precepts (*śīla*) simply mean the restraint and prohibition of all unwholesome dharmas;
if one does not commit evil, this is called "maintaining the precepts.

The *Sāṃghāṭasūtra* clarifies them through five meanings, as explained previously in terms of "restraint" (*saṃvara*), "narrowing" (*saṃvṛti*), "coolness" (*śīta*), "superiority" (*uttama*), and "training" (*śikṣā*).
Regarding the third point, the nature and characteristics of emergence,
there are differing views in the two treatises;
here, we shall follow our own school and provide an explanation based on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
First, the nature of the precept through formal action (*karmavācanā*) is clarified.
The treatise states:
"It takes the volition (*cetanā*) of bodily and vocal karma as its essence."
Regarding the body and speech, they are merely the instruments for creating good and evil.
Why is this so? For example, if a person kills a living being without intent, they do not incur the sin of killing; therefore, we know that the mind constitutes the essence [of action].
The text states:
"These three types of karma are all merely mind;
apart from the mind, there is no volition, and thus no karma of body or speech."
If one were to claim that physical form (*rūpa*) constitutes the essence of karma, this interpretation would be incorrect;
for the fourteen types of form are all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and do not possess the nature of either demerit or merit.

Furthermore, there are other masters who maintain that the essence of the *kṛta-śīla* (vow of action) consists in the continuity of wholesome forms and sounds produced by the two actions of body and speech.

Because it consists of a continuity of form and sound, is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), and is apprehended by the mental consciousness, it possesses the nature of either demerit or merit.
As for what is called "unmanifest precept" (*avijñapti-śīla*), its essence is neither form nor mind.
That which is non-material (*arūpa*) is not composed of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), as demonstrated by five points:

first, material form possesses spatial dimensions and location; second, material form has fourteen or twenty distinct varieties; third, material form is subject to affliction and destruction; fourth, material form is characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*); and fifth, material form is the object apprehended by the five consciousnesses.
Since non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) lacks these characteristics, it is known to be non-material.
Regarding the statement that it is "not mind": its essence is not characterized by discursive cognition (*ālambana*), and thus it is called "not mind.

Furthermore, there are five proofs for this: first, mind is characterized by deliberative knowledge; second, mind possesses both clarity and obscurity; third, mind encompasses the three moral natures; fourth, mind has both extensive and concise aspects; fifth, mind is a resultant phenomenon (*vipāka-dharma*);
non-informative action (*avijñapti*) does not possess these characteristics.
Therefore, the third aggregate has as its essence that which is neither form nor mind.
As the text states:

"As it is said in the Sūtras, a person who practices diligence attains a long life; following this long life, they obtain much merit; because of this great merit, they long experience celestial bliss."
If it were merely a wholesome mind, how could one obtain much merit?
This is because such a person cannot maintain a wholesome mind at all times.
Furthermore, the mental faculty lacks the restraint of the precepts.
If a person is in a state of unwholesome or neutral mind, they are still said to be "observing the precepts"; therefore, we know that at such times there is no active performance [of the act].
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"As for the precepts, although they lack the physical form of the precepts, they can still be guarded and maintained."
Although it is not something that can be physically contacted, through the skillful cultivation of expedient means, it can be fully attained.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:
"There are two kinds of precepts: the 'informative' (vijñapti) is material form (*rūpa*), while the 'non-informative' (avijñapti) is not material form."
Therefore, by means of numerous scriptural passages, it is established that [the precepts] are not material form (*rūpa*).
Fourth, the clarification of the sequence of the two types of precepts.
The initial explanation states:
It is like the two horns of an ox, which arise simultaneously.
Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun) states:
"In the very first moment of the precepts, both teachings exist together."
In the second moment of thought, there is only the non-informative (avijñapti).
The subsequent commentary states:
it arises both before and after.
Therefore, the *Sujāta-sūtra* states:
"In the laws of the world, where there is a cause, there is an effect;
just as when there is water or a mirror, there is the reflection of a face."
Thus we know that the manifest action (*vijñapti*) arises first, while the non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) arises later.
The *Śāstra* states:

"When at the time of the manifest action, both the manifest and the non-manifest are present," meaning that this is the non-manifest action coexisting with the manifest; both are causes of the precept.

Upon the completion of the third *karmavācanā*, the karma is fulfilled; thus, both these types of precepts are perfected, which is why it is said that they possess both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
This does not preclude the existence of the unmanifest that co-exists with the physical form, which nonetheless arises subsequently.
Furthermore, it is at the conclusion of a single thought-moment, after the two types of restraint have ceased, that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arises.
Fifth, a general explanation of its extent.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣikā-śāstra*, there are eight kinds of non-informative action:
First, there is the simultaneous non-manifesting (avijñapti).
For example, when one performs the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—they arise simultaneously with the preparatory effort (prayoga).
Second, there is the non-manifesting [karma] of both forms.
Just as with the vows of good and evil, when the physical form perishes, the precepts are lost;
yet these three matters persist in the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
Just as when a gift is not destroyed, the unmanifest continues to follow, so too do merits constantly arise from such things as monasteries, stupas, statues, bridges, and wells.
There are three conditions that preclude [the practice]:
first, if the previous matter has been ruined; second, if this person dies; third, if they give rise to false views.
In the absence of these three, the matter remains constant.
The same applies to evil conditions.
Fourth is non-action through application:
for example, if one dons the robe of giving and enters various meditative concentrations, it causes the donor to obtain immeasurable merit.
The power of the bowstring of adverse conditions can be understood by analogy with this.
Fifth is non-manifest action (avijñapti) through different conditions:
for example, when the body performs a verbal action, it gives rise to verbal non-manifest action;
The mouth creates bodily karma, giving rise to the non-informative (avijñapti) of the body, and so forth.
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*, the body and mouth create [karma] for one another.
There are six types of auxiliary conditions for non-informative karma.
Just as when one instructs another to kill or steal, the instructor incurs the offense at the moment the life is severed or the object is removed from its place.
The seventh is the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) based on a formal commitment, which is also called the non-informative action of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-avijñapti*).
Just as when a person makes a vow to hold a feast, to make robes, or to perform other acts of giving, non-informative action (*avijñapti*) constantly arises.
Eighth is non-informative action that follows the mind:
when there is a mind of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), non-informative action constantly arises; this is also called "concomitant with the mind."
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"Because one always possesses a virtuous mind during both entry and exit, it becomes increasingly superior.

This statement regarding "following the mind" means following the mind of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), wherein there is always non-informative action (*avijñapti*); it does not mean following meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*).
The Pratimokṣa is not like this; it follows only the body.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If one who has attained the first fruit is born in an evil land, the power of the Path prevents them from committing evil."
Among the eight types mentioned above, the first seven pertain to both wholesome and unwholesome states and are dharmas bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The latter one is non-informative (*avijñapti*); if it is mundane dhyāna, it is restricted to the two upper realms;
if it is the dharma of the supramundane path, it is not karma of the three realms.
Second, regarding the conformity and difference of the two types of experience:
the two kinds of non-action (avijñapti) are identical in five respects;
first, their names are identical.
"Receiving" (śīla) and "following" (anuśīla) are both termed "unmanifest reception" (avijñapti-śīla); this refers to the essence of the precepts within the ritual arena.
"Following" refers to the mind that guards the precepts toward objects after the initial reception; because it is skillfully accomplished through expedient means, it is called "original purity."
Second, they are identical in meaning, as both prevent the seven types of misconduct.
Third, they are identical in substance, as both take that which is neither form nor mind as their substance.
Fourth, they are identical in their opposition to what is not [the restraint].
Within the non-informative (avijñapti) nature of the precepts, there is a prevention directed toward specific objects, which is equal to the non-informative nature within the subsequent [moments].
These five categories share the same principle.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the attainment of the precepts arises repeatedly; whether they are robust or feeble is not fixed.
There are four types of difference:

first, the general arousal within the stage of undertaking [the precepts], wherein one attains them all collectively through the mental state of aspiration, as this pertains to the nature of the mind rather than the objective conditions;

second, the non-manifesting [precept] within the stage of following [the training], which arises individually, for practice is not undertaken instantaneously but is accomplished gradually and successively.
Second, they differ in their duration.
The non-informative (avijñapti) within the category of undertaking (samādāna) is projected in anticipation of a single form;

the non-informative within the category of following (anuvartana), however, arises simultaneously with the material factors and the mind of the preparatory means, and ceases when the activity stops; therefore, it is called "short."
Third, they differ in their breadth and narrowness:
within the category of sensation (*vedanā*), the three natures are always present by way of spontaneity;
whereas [the other categories] are restricted to the nature of goodness, and thus the two types of non-existence are termed "narrow."
The four faculties and the two branches are distinct.
Feeling (vedanā) is the root;
because they arise in dependence upon feeling, they are called branches.
The two types of agents have five similarities:

first, similarity of name; second, similarity of meaning; third, similarity of substance; fourth, similarity of brevity; and fifth, similarity of narrowness; they are restricted solely to the nature of the wholesome.
From this we can infer that there are four kinds of distinctions: first,
general abandonment within the category of "feeling" (vedanā), and specific abandonment within the category of "concomitants" (anuśaya).
The second type of reception is fundamental, following the specific branches.
The third type of reception is a preemptive defense, corresponding to the specific antidotes within each category.
The fourth type of reception constitutes a single stage, proceeding until the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), and thus conforms to the certainty of each respective stage.

Within the intermediate category of precepts, there are many varieties; because the fields and objects vary in quality and the mind varies in intensity, the mind is divided into three grades. This does not preclude the fact that the original undertaking may have been made with a mind of the lowest grade.
Therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"An Arhat possesses the lower grade of precepts, while a young bhikṣu possesses the upper grade of precepts.
This refers to the breadth or narrowness of the objective conditions from which the precepts of the three types of clear knowledge (*traividyā*) arise.

This is divided into four parts:
first, the cognizing mind, which takes as its object the present continuous stream of consciousness;
second, the perceived object.
Objects of perception span the three periods of time and are like enemies; even though an object has passed away, one can still give rise to an evil mind and sever a corpse.
A present enemy’s child possesses the quality of being destructible, and future objects may be understood by analogy therewith.
Therefore, the precepts are generated by taking the three periods of time as their objective conditions.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* asks:
Is the restraint (saṃvara) obtained only with respect to the present, or is it obtained from sentient beings of the three time periods?
It answers:
The sentient beings of the three periods of time obtain [this merit].
Just as a person who makes offerings to those honored in the past also gains merit,
so it is with the code of discipline (vinaya).
Third, regarding the arising of the precepts: they are obtained within the mind as it continues in the present moment.

Question:
Since the *vinaya* (discipline) has already arisen to extinguish [transgressions], while the precepts have not yet arisen to prevent them, how can it be said that past non-virtue is severed?
Answer:
Although the object has passed away, it is not the case that it is not past; thus, the precept still prevents the arising of transgression.
Another interpretation states:
first, through single-minded diligence one does not commit an offense; this is the precept preventing the arising of transgression.
Second, having committed an offense, one is able to repent and restore the purity of the precepts; this immediately eliminates the fault already incurred.
The remainder is explained as in the *Jieben shu* (Commentary on the Prātimokṣa).

Thus, while the objective conditions pertain to the three periods of time, the offense is incurred in the present; regarding the two periods of the past and future, one can only give rise to the thought, which is why it is said that the offense is "initiated" throughout the three periods.
If one bases this on the attainment of precepts, it exists only in the single moment of the present.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"Compassion and giving are likewise meritorious."
The precepts may also be understood in this way, for they extend across the three periods of time and are all associated with the intention to bring happiness.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The merit of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) encompasses all things, yet it pertains only to the present; the past and future have already passed away."
The precepts are not like that; they must necessarily be universal. If one acts with partiality or narrow-mindedness, it is entirely improper.
Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:
"Because the evil mind varies in its increase or decrease according to the precepts."
Question:
Is it that precepts arise from the three periods of time, yet only prevent non-virtue in two periods?
Answer:
If one discusses the substance of restraint itself, it cannot prevent wrongdoing alone; it is merely an instrument of prevention.
It must be upheld by the practitioner and employed as an auxiliary to the precepts before it can effectively guard against what is non-virtuous.
One does not guard against the present because there is nothing wrong with it.
If one lacks the sustained mind, one immediately forms sinful karma;
if one possesses right mindfulness, transgressions will not arise.
Furthermore, by following the reception of the material basis (*upadhi*), one ensures that what is not yet due to arise does not arise; thus, it prevents what is not yet [due].
If there were no such reception, nothing would arise accordingly.
Once evil karma has arisen, it is termed a transgression;
to protect the receptacle of the body so that it is not defiled by sensory dust,
and to repent and eliminate past karma, is termed guarding against transgressions.
If that is so, since precepts must necessarily prevent what is non-virtuous, why does such non-virtue arise at all?
Answer:
It is only when a practitioner, in accordance with the intermediate skillful means, maintains and resists [the arising of faults] that it can be called the "prevention of non-virtue."
This is like the analogy of city walls, moats, bows, and swords used to ward off and strike down enemies;

The *Sarvāstivāda* says:
Even with respect to those who are not sentient beings, one obtains immeasurable merit from the virtue of precepts.
For example, if one were to injure or damage as many things as there are dust motes throughout the trichiliocosm, down to the very limits of the earth, one would incur that much sin;

"The great earth is boundless; the precepts are likewise boundless."

Inferring from this, it is precisely because the ordained monks and nuns, as well as those of the three lower assemblies, uphold the vessel of preceptual virtue and follow the traces of the sages in their conduct, that they occupy a station superior to that of gods and humans.
Maintaining oneself in dignified composure, one's merit and virtue flow perpetually.
Thus, the *Vidyāmātrasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Forty-two thousand rivers of merit flow eternally."
The commentary states:
This refers to the forty-two thousand rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), which flow constantly like a river to wash away the afflictions of broken precepts.
As for the number "forty-two thousand," it means that there are four hundred and twenty root precepts.
The reason for this is as follows: in the *Vasudharmā-vinaya*, there are two hundred precepts, most of which clarify minor rules;
in the *Upadeśa*, there are one hundred and twenty-one precepts, most of which clarify major rules;
and the specific precepts for bhikṣuṇīs number ninety-nine.
In total, there are four hundred and twenty [instances].
Each individual precept possesses ten merits, such as the "gathering of the Saṃgha" and so forth;

each of these merits can give rise to ten kinds of right practices, namely: the five faculties beginning with faith, the three roots of goodness beginning with non-attachment, and the two types of restraint regarding body and speech.
One precept is equivalent to one hundred; thus, they combine to form four hundred and twenty, which is not indeed forty-two thousand.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:

"The Vinaya of No-Vow" (apraṇihita-vinaya) means that when the third *karmavācanā* is completed, the forty-two thousand rules of training arise simultaneously; because there is not a single precept that does not arise, it is called "No-Vow."
Seeking the truth based on this, the virtue of the precepts flows perpetually.
